The field now: who is working on what

Roughly 420 researchers published on the Indus civilisation, its script and its neighbours in the past year, across these 8 directions.

Past 12 months, updated 19 November 2026. Bars show distinct authors; lines show papers per year (the dashed end is this year so far). These are estimates from keyword matches, not a census.

How we counted

Counts are estimates from keyword matches in OpenAlex titles and abstracts (journal articles, reviews and book chapters; self-archived preprints left out because they include many unreviewed decipherment claims), for the 12 months to the update date. A paper can match more than one direction, and the headline removes people counted twice. Distinct authors and institutions are exact up to 400 papers per direction and extrapolated from the newest 400 above that. Each direction lists its exact query so anyone can check it.

Dataset12 Nov 2026

An open test for filling in missing signs

Kanichira, Singam, Katyal and Somala (IIT Hyderabad) · Zenodo 24164070

A team released code, data and predictions for a model that guesses damaged or missing signs.

Many seals are chipped, so some signs are lost. This team trained a model to fill the gaps and published everything: the code, how they split the texts for training and testing, and the model’s guesses. Because it is all open, anyone can check how good it really is.

Neural masked-sign restoration with public train/test splits and predictions (CC BY 4.0 and MIT, about 6 MB). The record page does not describe the corpus or the model. The main risk is leakage: near-copies of the same seal text can sit on both sides of a split, which inflates scores.

Tested

What we take from it: We graded it, then retrained their own code. 36% of its test texts have a near-copy (one sign off, or contained) in its training texts. Training without those near-copies lowers every model’s first-guess accuracy by about 6-7 points, compared with dropping the same number of unrelated texts. Without them, the neural model still does no better than their simple three-sign model.

Read the full summary: An open test for filling in missing signs →
Preprint9 Nov 2026

Cold War spy photos show when Haryana’s Indus mounds were built over

Gerrits, Petrie and colleagues (Cambridge, Arkansas) · Research Square preprint

Declassified 1975 satellite photos fill the gap between 1915 maps and today for 12 Harappan sites in Haryana.

Old maps from 1915 and modern satellite images leave a 100-year gap. Spy photos taken in 1975 fill it. By 1975 most uncultivated land around the mounds was already farmed. At Rakhigarhi the village had grown over the mounds mostly before 1975.

Six KH-9 Hexagon frames georeferenced in the Sunspot tool; land cover in 1915, 1975 and 2021 around 12 sites. Non-cropland fell from 35% to 14% to 4% of the observed area. Built-up land within 1 km of Rakhigarhi: 3.9%, 19.5%, 23.7%. Sirsa reached 75.1% by 2021. Preprint; site rasters withheld to protect sites.

Background

What we take from it: What survives to be dug up, seals included, depends on what was destroyed first. When we compare inscription counts across Haryana sites, site loss belongs in the model as a covariate.

Read the full summary: Cold War spy photos show when Haryana’s Indus mounds were built over →
Preprint12 Oct 2026

One sign that never follows another

Dominik · Zenodo 23307028

A paper on sign grammar makes one sharp claim that can be checked in minutes.

Most of the paper’s grammar gain is tiny. But it makes one clear claim: a certain sign never comes right after the arrow sign, yet often comes right after the jar sign. A rule that sharp is easy to test on texts the author did not use.

Held-out gain of only 0.014 nats per sign (CI 0.010 to 0.018) on 6,778 tokens, and the author notes the contexts were chosen in advance. Sharp claim, in Wells numbers: W090 never follows W520 (0 of 136) but follows W740 in 69 of 994 cases (7%). The corpus inputs are withheld.

Tested

What we take from it: We tested it. The pattern shows in reading order on the main texts, but not on texts kept aside, and gaps this sharp are common: 24 of 57 similar sign pairs have one. So it is real but not special.

Read the full summary: One sign that never follows another →
Preprint5 Oct 2026

Where Indus texts wrap to a new line can be ranked, but carries little information

Zenil and Uthamacumaran · arXiv 2610.08861

A study of five undeciphered records finds Indus line breaks are predictable in rank but weak in bits.

The authors asked what can be learned about undeciphered records without reading them: layout, word division, reading direction. They tested Indus texts, the Phaistos disc, rongorongo, khipu and the Voynich manuscript, with Egyptian as a control. For Indus, a model could often tell which gap was a line break. But the amount of information in that prediction was tiny.

Algorithmic-information and predictive-coding measures with held-out records and 999 null draws. Indus: 292 gaps in 47 multi-line inscriptions from a derivative CSV, 49 of them row breaks, Mohenjo-daro held out. Row-break AUC 0.812 (bootstrap 0.742-0.871) but a code gain of only 0.0092 bits per gap; rongorongo AUC 0.51, Egyptian 0.95. The Indus test is small and uses slash delimiters, not measured positions. Preprint.

Background

What we take from it: It touches our line_breaks test, which asks whether breaks fall at slot boundaries. Their gap between a good ranking and almost no information is a warning for our attacks too: report both accuracy and bits. They also say any search over languages and settings must sit inside the train/test split, which is how the mismatch study is sealed.

Read the full summary: Where Indus texts wrap to a new line can be ranked, but carries little information →
PreprintOct 2026

A fair way to ask “is this a language?”

Zhang and Sheng · arXiv 2610.34499

Give both explanations the same effort, then judge them on text neither has seen.

Is the Voynich manuscript a hidden language, or meaningless copying? The authors write each explanation as a machine that produces text, give both machines the same amount of tuning, and score them on pages kept aside. They checked the method on 28 texts in 16 languages and on planted messages.

Both hypotheses (meaningless copying vs enciphered language) are written as generative programs, fitted with the same search budget and compared on held-out statistics. Adds a decipherment-free signal (the same word pairs keep sharing a line), calibrated on 28 texts in 16 languages plus planted messages. No code link. The line signal does not transfer: Indus texts average 4.6 signs on a single line.

Using it

What we take from it: The equal-effort, held-out rule is now our standard for any reopened “language or code” test.

Read the full summary: A fair way to ask “is this a language?” →
PaperOct 2026

Some sign statistics carry over between languages that share a script; others break

Zhou and Anderson · EMNLP 2026

Word-splitting methods trained on one cuneiform language mostly still work on another, until foreign word-signs appear.

Cuneiform wrote several unrelated languages, among them Akkadian, Sumerian and Elamite. The authors asked which patterns belong to the script and which to each language. A simple method that splits text where the next sign is hard to predict kept working across languages. It failed badly on Hittite, where about a third of the signs are word-signs borrowed from other languages.

Two dictionary-free segmenters (transitional probability, Morfessor) on ORACC Akkadian, ETCSL Sumerian and Elamite; six cross-language pairs. Within language both reach F1 above 0.97 against 0.74 for a dictionary baseline. Transitional probability stays above 0.95 F1 across all six pairs; Morfessor falls to 0.27 when trained on the 13K-token Elamite source. On Hittite, with 34.7% foreign-script logograms, transitional probability drops 35 points. Segmentation and tagging, not decipherment.

Background

What we take from it: This bears on the mismatch study’s logo-syllabic arm. Borrowed word-signs are a kind of mismatch of their own, different from a related language. A “foreign logograms” variant in the logogram-share slice would test it; nothing in the sealed stage 1 changes.

Read the full summary: Some sign statistics carry over between languages that share a script; others break →
Paper20 Aug 2026

Isotopes suggest cattle reached Gujarat from far away, perhaps Haryana

Mahala, Laskar and colleagues · Journal of Quaternary Science

Teeth and bone at Kanmer and Tigrana show local sheep and goats but some non-local cattle at Kanmer.

Chemical traces in teeth record where an animal grew up. The team tested animals from two Harappan sites more than 900 km apart. Sheep and goats were raised locally. Some cattle at Kanmer in Gujarat seem to have come from elsewhere, likely Haryana.

C-O-Sr-Nd isotopes on faunal teeth, bone bioapatite and bone-encased soil from Kanmer (Gujarat) and Tigrana (Haryana). Most sheep and goat local; bovines from Mature and late-Mature Kanmer of diverse, possibly non-local origin, “likely” Haryana. Local rainfall was the main water source at Kanmer. No sample counts seen (abstract only).

Background

What we take from it: A physical link between Gujarat and Haryana is one channel for shared seal practice. Kanmer has excavated seals and sealings. A test: do Kanmer texts share more sign sequences with Haryana sites than distance predicts?

Preprint17 Aug 2026

A calibrated attack finds no language behind the Voynich manuscript’s units

Rozanova and Temerev · arXiv 2608.17096

Tested first on ciphers with a known answer, the attack recovers Latin with the right model and little with a wrong one, and Voynich looks like the wrong-language case.

Before attacking the Voynich text, the authors built ciphers of Latin where they knew the answer. With a Latin model their attack recovered most of the key. With a German model it recovered little. They also compared each real text with a fake one that copies its letter patterns. The Voynich text scored no better than its fake, like the wrong-language case.

Multi-glyph units learned by BPE and class merging, then a class-to-letter substitution attack against seven language models, with eight restarts. On synthetic Latin homophonic ciphers it recovers 73.7-92.6% of the frequency-weighted mapping with the right model and 0-23.4% with the wrong (German) one. The real-minus-surrogate differential is positive in all 25 right-language runs (+0.13 to +0.52); Voynich gives a mean of -0.0085. Wrong-language arm is one language; calibrated for concatenative ciphers only.

Background

What we take from it: This is close to our mismatch study. Their wrong-language result is one more point on our curve: low recovery when the model is the wrong language. Their fake-text comparison (a generator fitted to the same corpus) is a stronger null than our shuffled negative, and we should add it next to planted check PC3.

Read the full summary: A calibrated attack finds no language behind the Voynich manuscript’s units →
Preprint7 Aug 2026

A new model fills gaps in damaged Greek inscriptions better than earlier ones

Cullhed and Thörn Cleland · arXiv 2608.07249

A letter-level model restores damaged Greek inscriptions with fewer errors than Ithaca and Aeneas, and every test has a matched control.

Many Greek inscriptions are broken. This team trained a large model to guess missing letters. Each experiment was repeated with an untrained copy of the model, so the gain from training is clear. They also released versions that never saw each passage, so tests are fair.

Stoicheia: a 405M-parameter character-level masked-diffusion encoder trained on 380M words, released as ten rotated decontaminated folds plus one. Pretraining adds 5.6 CER points on inscription reconstruction against a random-initialisation control. On Ithaca’s test split character error falls from 24.6 (Ithaca) and 23.5 (Aeneas) to 15.5, and top-1 accuracy rises from 63.0 and 64.0 to 74.5 (abstract only). Greek has a huge corpus; Indus does not.

Background

What we take from it: We took the testing habits, not the model. Our sign-restoration benchmark already keeps near-copies out of the test set. Rotating folds, so every text is unseen by one released model, and a matched untrained control are two checks to add.

Read the full summary: A new model fills gaps in damaged Greek inscriptions better than earlier ones →
PreprintAug 2026

An invented symbol system with no sounds looks just like the Indus script

Raghavendra · arXiv 2608.02999 (SIGIL)

If a made-up emblem system matches every statistic, statistics alone cannot prove the signs are writing.

He built an artificial system of emblems with no language behind it. It matched the Indus script on every measure he could compute exactly. Programs that “decode” by matching dictionaries happily read it as English, Sanskrit or Tamil. So those numbers cannot settle whether the Indus signs write a language.

SIGIL is a sound-free emblem generator matched to Indus on every exactly scorable statistic (entropy, Zipf, n-grams, positional concentration). Dictionary-hit decoders produce fluent readings of it in several languages. This closes entropy- and Zipf-style arguments in both directions.

Using it

What we take from it: Every new claim we test must also fail on SIGIL-style emblem data. We use it as a standing negative control.

Read the full summary: An invented symbol system with no sounds looks just like the Indus script →
Paper23 Jul 2026

Indus-style farming went on in the Ghaggar basin after the 4.2 ka drought

Swaroop, Srivastava and colleagues · Vegetation History and Archaeobotany

Directly dated crops at Jognakhera, a Bara-culture site, show the Indus crop package continuing after the drought.

About 4,200 years ago a long drought hit the region. At Jognakhera, farmers afterwards still grew the same summer and winter crops as Indus farmers. A directly dated rice grain hints at contact with the Ganga plain. The authors read this as continuity and an eastward move of people, not collapse.

Macrobotanical analysis with direct dating of grains and seeds; settlement 4,300-3,400 yr BP; the Bara culture emerged around 2300 BCE, alongside the late Urban phase. Winter and summer crops, legumes in both seasons (crop rotation), a directly dated rice grain. One site; “migration” is inferred from material similarity (abstract only).

Background

What we take from it: Late inscriptions are rare. This supports asking whether writing faded with the cities or moved east with the people. It also helps date late-phase objects.

Paper18 Jul 2026

A short book on proto-Elamite, the Indus script’s other unread neighbour

Kelley · Cambridge Elements

A new overview of proto-Elamite: about 1,700 tablets from Iran, c. 3300-2900 BCE, still only partly read.

Proto-Elamite was written in Iran about 5,000 years ago, mostly to count goods, people and institutions. It is only partly understood. This short book sums up what is known. It describes a decipherment effort that mixes mathematics, comparison with other scripts and computer methods.

Cambridge Element; about 1,700 clay tablets, c. 3300-2900 BCE, hundreds of signs. The abstract describes the decipherment as combining mathematics, comparative studies, corpus digitisation and computer science (abstract only).

Background

What we take from it: Proto-Elamite is the closest working model for an undeciphered administrative script. We use the computational methods of the same group in our Elamite bridge. The book is now the reference to check for sign-value anchors usable as a logo-syllabic test case.

Read the full summary: A short book on proto-Elamite, the Indus script’s other unread neighbour →
Paper30 Jun 2026

A first dig at a new Rakhigarhi mound finds a stamp seal in dated late layers

Gupta and Kumar · Vestigia Indica (BSSS journal)

The 2021-22 season at Rakhigarhi mound 3 found houses, burials, beads, a gold piece and one steatite seal, dated c. 2000-1800 BCE.

Rakhigarhi is one of the largest Indus cities. This report covers the first season on its mound 3. Diggers found mud and fired-brick buildings, child and adult burials, beads, figurines, a piece of gold and one stone seal. Radiocarbon dates put the layers late in the city’s life, about 2000-1800 BCE.

First-season report, RGR-3, 2021-22. Mud and burnt-brick structures, child and adult burials, steatite and carnelian beads, terracotta figurines, a gold fragment and a steatite seal. AMS dates: late Mature to Late Harappan, c. 2000-1800 BCE. The abstract does not describe the seal or its text. Small regional journal; issue dated June 2026, DOI registered November 2026 (abstract only).

Waiting on data

What we take from it: A seal with a known mound and a dated late phase is the kind of record our find-spot and date tests need. If its inscription is published, it becomes a late-phase test case for our chronology work.

Paper18 May 2026

House sizes show inequality fell over time in Mohenjo-daro

Green, Alam and Petrie · Antiquity

Gini scores of house areas at Mohenjo-daro fell over time, as the city grew more prosperous.

Many early cities had rich and poor districts. The authors measured the floor area of 162 Mohenjo-daro houses as a rough guide to wealth. Inequality was lower than in Mesopotamian cities. In one area it fell over time as the street plan developed.

Gini coefficients of residence area from early excavation plans. Overall Gini 0.44 (n = 162), below Ur and Ugarit (above 0.6). In area DK-G South it fell from 0.39 (c. 2500 BC) to 0.23 (c. 2100 BC). Old plans with weak stratigraphy; house area is only a proxy for wealth.

Background

What we take from it: Seals are often read as marks of elite power. DK-G South has both phased houses and many seals, so seal counts per house can be set against house size. That tests whether seal use tracked wealth.

PaperMay 2026

Testing rongorongo as a syllable script: even the same language in another style halves recovery

Korovina · LT4HALA 2026 (LREC)

A syllable-substitution attack works on enciphered Rapa Nui text, fails on rongorongo, and loses most of its power when the model comes from another genre.

Rongorongo is the undeciphered script of Easter Island. The author first tested an attack on Rapa Nui texts turned into code, where the answer is known. With statistics from the same kind of text, it recovered most syllables. With statistics from another kind of text in the same language, it recovered far fewer. On real rongorongo it scored at the level of noise.

Genetic-algorithm substitution attack scored by unigram, bigram and trigram counts; five Rapa Nui sub-corpora; 1,000-syllable fragments. Same-corpus model: about 26 syllables recovered, over 80% text coverage. Other-genre model: 10 syllables and 37%; worst pair (Manuscript E text, Gospel of Matthew model) 4.6. A pooled model of all five gives 17 and 62%. Fitness correlates 0.75 with accuracy; below 2,500,000 points is noise, and rongorongo scores 1.0M-1.3M. One fragment length; no spread reported.

Background

What we take from it: This matters for the mismatch study. Its “same language across genres” pairs are not near-zero mismatch: genre alone cut recovery by more than half here. The true-model control must use the same genre as the text, and each genre pair needs its own measured mismatch. A pooled-genre model is a cheap way to narrow the gap.

Read the full summary: Testing rongorongo as a syllable script: even the same language in another style halves recovery →
PreprintApr 2026

The Indus script sits between coats of arms and paperwork

Nair · arXiv 2604.17828

Compared with made-up systems of known kinds, Indus falls between heraldry and administrative records.

The author built artificial sign systems of different kinds, such as coats of arms and office records, and compared their statistics with the Indus texts. The Indus script lands between the two.

A synthetic-baseline scorecard: generated heraldic, administrative and linguistic corpora scored on shared statistics. Indus sits between heraldic and administrative baselines.

Background

What we take from it: Agrees with our finding that each kind of object has its own vocabulary. Nothing new to run.

Read the full summary: The Indus script sits between coats of arms and paperwork →
NewsApr 2026

Reported: a new seal with Indus signs from the UAE

News report (no excavation report yet) · Umm al-Quwain, UAE

A round Gulf-style seal with Indus signs and a humped bull, dated to about 2300 BCE. Not yet verified.

A news site reports a small round seal of the Gulf type, with Indus signs and a humped bull, from Umm al-Quwain. The excavation report, the exact find spot and a readable photo of the signs have not been published, so we cannot use it yet.

Known only from a news aggregator. Site (possibly Tell Abraq), excavator and sign sequence not given. Not in our corpus of objects found abroad.

Waiting on data

What we take from it: We looked for an excavation report and found none, and the news page is now offline. It stays out of our data until the find is published.

Read the full summary: Reported: a new seal with Indus signs from the UAE →
PreprintMar 2026

The “registration code” reading fails its own predictions

Kriger and Hunt · Zenodo 19103880

They argued seal texts work like ID numbers. On 646 seals, the texts repeat more than chance, not less.

This preprint argued that seal texts are like registration numbers: each one unique, with numbers in fixed places. We ran their tests on 646 Mohenjo-daro unicorn seals. The texts turned out less unique than chance, and the number patterns did not hold.

Uniqueness 88.2% vs 99.2% under random redeal (below every null draw). Numerals in the second-to-last slot 19.0% vs 18.7% shuffled (p = 0.46). Their dominant “2” is mostly the M99 connective of the opening formula. Near-duplicates differ at an edge in 20 of 80 pairs, so “never at edges” is false. The edge pattern in positional entropy replicates, but it was already known.

Closed

What we take from it: Nothing to borrow. Their best result was already known, and the rest fails.

Read the full summary: The “registration code” reading fails its own predictions →
Book2026

The full edition of Linear Elamite, the script read through kings’ names

Desset and colleagues · Linear Elamite Texts from Susa (OrientLab SM 10)

All the Susa texts of the script read in 2022, the most recent ancient script to be read.

Linear Elamite, from what is now Iran, was read in 2022. The key was royal names already known from cuneiform, on objects dated well enough to predict which names should appear. This book publishes the full set of texts from Susa.

Complete edition of the Susa Linear Elamite texts. The decipherment (Desset et al. 2022, ZA 112:11-60) is anchored on royal names and titles known from cuneiform. Critics question parts of it: Dahl 2023 (archaising, not purely syllabic) and Mäder (about 70% phonetic).

Tested

What we take from it: We used Linear Elamite as a known-answer test for our own name-matching method. The method could not recover its values, so we stopped it rather than run it on Indus.

Read the full summary: The full edition of Linear Elamite, the script read through kings’ names →
Event20 Aug 2025

India’s archaeology agency held a three-day meeting on the script

Archaeological Survey of India · Decipherment of Indus Script: Current Status and Way Forward, 20–22 Aug 2025

A national meeting on the state of decipherment. No proceedings yet.

The Archaeological Survey of India brought researchers together for three days to review where decipherment stands. Only the programme is public so far.

Programme only. No proceedings or papers found as of November 2026.

Waiting on data

What we take from it: We have asked the agency whether readings proposed there can be scored on our open test bench.

Read the full summary: India’s archaeology agency held a three-day meeting on the script →
PaperMay 2025

Teaching computers to find signs and animals in seal photos

Dixit and colleagues · Journal of Computer Applications in Archaeology 8(1):156–169

Image models that spot signs and animal motifs on photographs of seals.

The team trained image models to find the signs on a seal photo, name each one, and recognise the animal. Only sample data is public. The full set is available from the authors on request.

YOLOv3 sign detection, MobileNet sign classification and motif identification on seal photographs. The repository (DM-BiCLab) holds sample data only.

Idea, needs data

What we take from it: Reading signs straight from photos could settle the 1-in-8 disagreements between the two main transcriptions. We need open images first.

Read the full summary: Teaching computers to find signs and animals in seal photos →
PreprintMar 2025

Do Indus signs look more like scripts from the Himalayas than from Mesopotamia?

ivc2tyc project · arXiv 2503.21074

An image-AI comparison claims Tibetan-Yi corridor scripts resemble Indus signs most.

Using image AI, the authors compare sign shapes and report that scripts from the Tibetan-Yi corridor, such as Naxi Dongba and Yi, look more like Indus signs than proto-cuneiform or Proto-Elamite do. Looking alike does not mean sounding alike, but their open sign images are useful.

Hybrid vision embeddings over glyph image sets for Indus, proto-cuneiform, Proto-Elamite and five Tibetan-Yi scripts (GitHub oohalakkadi/ivc2tyc, MIT; recommended by PCI Archaeology). Shape similarity carries no sound values: Linear Elamite look-alikes failed blind (p = 0.83).

Tested

What we take from it: We red-teamed it. The claim technically survives, but its whole edge comes from one small script, Ba-Shu. Proto-cuneiform is closer to Indus than four of the five Himalayan scripts.

Read the full summary: Do Indus signs look more like scripts from the Himalayas than from Mesopotamia? →
StudyJan 2025

15,184 marks on South Indian pottery, many with Indus look-alikes

Rajan and Sivanantham (Tamil Nadu Archaeology) · Tamil Nadu graffiti study

Most pottery marks from 140 Tamil Nadu sites have a similar-looking Indus sign.

Archaeologists in Tamil Nadu catalogued 15,184 marks scratched on pots from 140 sites and found that most have an Indus sign that looks similar. The marks are about 1,000 years younger, and most stand alone rather than in texts.

Shape parallels for roughly 60–90% of marks. Gap of over 1,000 years; mostly single marks. Earlier work found that look-alike marks do not behave like the Indus signs they resemble.

Closed

What we take from it: We tested whether look-alikes behave alike. They do not, so this route is closed for now.

Read the full summary: 15,184 marks on South Indian pottery, many with Indus look-alikes →
Paper2025

How computers are opening up Proto-Elamite, the Indus script’s unread neighbour

Monroe, Kelley, Born and Sarkar · Near Eastern Archaeology 88(4):316–323, building on Born et al. 2019–2023

Without knowing the language, they found which signs head an entry, which are built from parts, and which number system each count uses.

Proto-Elamite, from Iran, is unread and about as old as the Indus script. Teams have used computers to learn how its texts are organised: which signs start an entry, which complex signs are made of simpler ones, and which counting system each number belongs to, by looking at what is being counted. None of this needs the language.

Born et al. (2019, 2021, 2023): topic models (LDA) for genres, “header” signs, complex-sign compositionality, and disambiguation of numerals by number system. These are the methods that worked on an undeciphered administrative script without a language. They have not been applied as a set to the Indus texts.

Tested

What we take from it: We tried the pieces that fit. Indus signs that look like Proto-Elamite or proto-cuneiform signs do not behave like them (0 of 5 tests), complex signs do not split into their parts, and no known number system matches the Indus counts. Still untried: letting a model find genres from scratch.

Read the full summary: How computers are opening up Proto-Elamite, the Indus script’s unread neighbour →

02Landmarks

The papers that shaped the field

Including two from other scripts whose methods we borrow.

Other scripts1960

Reading Maya history before reading a single sound

Tatiana Proskouriakoff · American Antiquity 25(4):454–475

She matched glyph patterns to the lifespans of rulers, and found births and accessions without sounding anything out.

Maya monuments carry dates. Proskouriakoff noticed that the dates on each group of monuments spanned a human lifetime, and that the same glyphs always sat beside a first date (birth) and a later one (taking the throne). So the texts were about real rulers. She worked out what glyphs meant from the pattern of events, years before anyone could read their sounds.

Pattern-of-dates analysis at Piedras Negras: recurring glyph-date pairings mapped onto plausible life events (birth, accession, death), with intervals constrained by human lifespans.

Tested

What we take from it: We tested it on the 1930s excavation registers. Seals found in streets carry the same signs as seals found in rooms, and broken seals carry the same signs as pieces of whole ones. Most other fates, such as burnt, buried or hoarded seals, are recorded too rarely to test. One small lead, that damaged seals keep more end signs, did not survive a second team: it came from damaged seals having shorter texts.

Read the full summary: Reading Maya history before reading a single sound →
Corpus1977

The list of every text that made the field possible

Iravatham Mahadevan · The Indus Script: Texts, Concordance and Tables

417 signs, numbered, and every text then known. The M-numbers on this site come from it.

Mahadevan drew every sign, gave each a number and listed every known inscription, with every place each sign appears. Almost all statistical work since, including ours, starts from this list.

Sign list of 417 signs with a full concordance of the texts then known. Showed the regular positions of signs, such as the jar sign usually ending a text. Allograph splitting differs from the later Wells/Fuls list (676–713 signs).

Using it

What we take from it: The backbone of our main transcription.

Read the full summary: The list of every text that made the field possible →
Book1994

The best-known case that the signs write an early Dravidian language

Asko Parpola · Deciphering the Indus Script (Cambridge University Press)

Fish sign = mīn, a word that means both “fish” and “star” in Dravidian languages.

Parpola argues the signs are mostly word-signs that also work like puns, the way a picture of a bee plus a leaf can spell “belief”. His famous example is the fish sign: in Dravidian languages the word mīn means both fish and star, so a number plus fish could name a star group.

Logo-syllabic, rebus-based Proto-Dravidian reading. Fish M59 = mīn “fish/star”; six + fish = aṟu-mīn (Pleiades); seven + fish = eḻu-mīn (Ursa Major); intersecting circles = muruku. About 400 signs is too many for a syllabary and too few for pure word-writing.

Tested

What we take from it: We turned his readings into predictions and tested them. Six + fish holds as a fixed unit; “seven stars” is not supported; the fish signs group together but do not behave like god names.

Read the full summary: The best-known case that the signs write an early Dravidian language →
Paper2004

The case that the signs might not be writing at all

Farmer, Sproat and Witzel · Electronic Journal of Vedic Studies 11(2)

Texts are very short, and many signs are rare: maybe these are symbols, not a script.

The authors pointed out that Indus texts are very short, about five signs on average, that many signs appear only once, and that no long text has ever been found. They argued the signs could be a system of symbols, like road signs or coats of arms, rather than writing that records speech.

Arguments from text length (mean about 4.6 signs, longest single-surface text 17), rare-sign frequency and the absence of long texts. Sparked the language-vs-symbols debate continued by Rao et al. 2009 and Sproat 2010 and 2014.

Using it

What we take from it: We test whether the signs are language at all, instead of assuming it.

Read the full summary: The case that the signs might not be writing at all →
Debate2009–2014

Does sign order prove it is a language? The numbers say no

Rao et al. 2009 (Science); Sproat 2010, 2014 (Language) · Science 324; Language 90:457

A measure of how predictable the next sign is put Indus near languages. Critics showed non-writing scores there too.

Rao’s team measured how predictable the next sign is and found the Indus script sits in the same band as languages. Sproat replied that symbol systems that are not writing can score the same way, and that two better measures put Indus with non-writing. Later work, including SIGIL, settled it: these numbers alone cannot decide.

Conditional entropy of sign bigrams (Rao et al. 2009); n-gram restoration of missing signs (Yadav et al. 2010, PLoS ONE). Sproat (2010, 2014): the entropy band does not separate writing from non-writing; two measures that do put Indus and Pictish on the non-linguistic side.

Closed

What we take from it: Treat entropy, Zipf and n-gram arguments as closed in both directions.

Read the full summary: Does sign order prove it is a language? The numbers say no →
Paper2010

Indus signs used in a new way on seals from the Gulf

Steffen Laursen · Arabian Archaeology and Epigraphy 21

Round seals from the Gulf use Indus signs in combinations rarely seen at home.

Traders around Bahrain made round seals of their own style but carved Indus signs on them. Laursen showed these seals use the signs differently, for example often putting a “twins” sign at the front. One explanation is that local names were written with borrowed signs.

Gulf-type round seals show an excess of the prefixed “twins” sign and sign pairs unseen at home. Suggests Indus signs adapted to another language in the Gulf.

Tested

What we take from it: Our round-seal finding builds on this, and adds that round seals found in Indus cities break the order too.

Read the full summary: Indus signs used in a new way on seals from the Gulf →
Other scripts2010–2019

Computers can crack a script, if they know a related language

Snyder, Barzilay and Knight 2010; Luo, Cao and Barzilay 2019 · ACL 2010; ACL 2019

Ugaritic and Linear B were re-deciphered by machine, but only by matching them to Hebrew and Greek.

Machine learning re-cracked two ancient scripts: Ugaritic, matched against Hebrew, and Linear B, matched against early Greek. The trick only works when you already know a closely related language. For the Indus script, no such language is known.

Snyder et al. 2010: 29 of 30 Ugaritic letters recovered via Hebrew cognates. Luo et al. 2019: 67.3% of Linear B cognates recovered via Greek. Luo et al. 2021 found no strong evidence that Basque is related to Iberian.

Closed

What we take from it: We tested the planted-language version at Indus size. Without the right language, it fails, so this route waits for an outside clue.

Read the full summary: Computers can crack a script, if they know a related language →
Genetics2019

DNA from Rakhigarhi: who the Indus people were

Shinde et al. (Cell); Narasimhan et al. (Science) · Cell 179; Science 365

One ancient genome: no steppe ancestry, and close links to later South Indian populations.

Scientists read the DNA of a person buried at the Indus city of Rakhigarhi. It had no ancestry from the Eurasian steppe, which arrived in South Asia later, and it is related to the main ancestry of later South Indians. That fits an Indus language that was not Indo-European, perhaps related to Dravidian, but genes do not prove a language.

Genome I6113 (1 of 61 skeletons screened): Iranian-related plus AASI ancestry, no steppe or Anatolian farmer ancestry. Narasimhan et al.: an “Indus Periphery Cline”; steppe ancestry arrives after about 2000 BCE.

Background

What we take from it: Background only. It narrows the likely language families but gives no sign values.

Read the full summary: DNA from Rakhigarhi: who the Indus people were →
Paper2019–2023

The texts as labels for goods and permits, not names

Bahata Ansumali Mukhopadhyay · Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (2019, 2021, 2023)

Stroke signs as units of measure, crop signs as goods, and no personal names.

Mukhopadhyay reads the inscriptions as practical labels: what a parcel holds, how much, and who may pass, rather than people’s names. Stroke signs would be units whose value depends on the goods, and some signs would stand for crops or other commodities. In 2025 she proposed the fish signs mean gems.

Logographic or semasiographic “formalised data carriers”: metrological strokes, commodity signs after numerals, the jar as a phrase-final function sign, Kanmer tablets as gate passes; pīlu “elephant/tooth” as a loanword (2021); fish = maṇi “gem” (2025, SSRN 5079207).

Next to test

What we take from it: A first test found no sign tied to a craft at two sites, but it had too little data to tell. The fish = gem prediction needs find spots from bead workshops, which we have asked excavators for.

Read the full summary: The texts as labels for goods and permits, not names →
Paper2022

Linear Elamite read, through kings’ names

Desset, Tabibzadeh, Kervran, Basello and Marchesi · Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 112:11–60

The most recent ancient script to be read, and a model of what the Indus script is missing.

The team read Linear Elamite by finding the names of kings they already knew from cuneiform, written on silver beakers that could be dated. Each name gave the sounds of several signs. The Indus script has no such object yet: no text in a known script that names an Indus person.

Anchored on royal names and titles from cuneiform on datable objects (silver gunagi beakers, Desset 2018). Critiques: Dahl 2023; Mäder; Kelley et al. 2022 call the proposed Proto-Elamite values premature.

Using it

What we take from it: This is why we search for names of people from the Indus region in cuneiform records, and asked museums for seal impressions on tablets that name them.

Read the full summary: Linear Elamite read, through kings’ names →
Other scripts2022

Letting the computer decide which shapes are the same sign

Corazza and colleagues · PLOS ONE (Cypro-Minoan)

Images plus context sorted Cypro-Minoan’s variant shapes into signs.

Scholars disagree about whether two similar shapes are one sign or two. For Cypro-Minoan, this team let a model look at each sign’s picture and where it appears, and group them. The Indus script has the same problem: the two main sign lists count about 400 and about 700 signs.

Sign2Vec: unsupervised clustering on image features plus distributional context, validated on Cypro-Minoan with known-answer checks.

Tested

What we take from it: We tried it on two older scripts whose sign lists are known. Shape plus context merged too many signs that are not the same, and context alone was almost always wrong. Shape alone did best. On the Indus texts, a shape-only list fits unseen texts a little better than the 400-sign list, but a second team found half of that gain is one choice (three fish shapes counted as one sign) and it did not repeat on texts found after 1977. So the texts do not settle the count. The 700 side cannot be tested at all: most of those extra signs appear once or twice.

Read the full summary: Letting the computer decide which shapes are the same sign →

    Grade the new sign-restoration model fairly, with near-copies kept out of its test setWe graded it, then retrained their own code. 36% of its test texts have a near-copy (one sign off, or contained) in its training texts.
